title: Interleaved Dequant Buffer Protocol for Streaming Low‑bit Execution
content:
Purpose:
This doc specifies a runtime protocol for interleaved dequantization buffers (IDB) designed to support low‑bit inference formats (INT8, FP8, GPTQ, AWQ) under streaming/long‑context workloads. The goal is to enable zero‑pause token streaming while preserving KV cache coherence across mixed precision kernels and multi‑GPU KV sharding.

Scope:
- Runtime buffer layout and lifecycle for partial dequantization of attention inputs and KV writes in streaming scenarios.
- Kernel ABI extensions and scheduling hooks required to use IDB.
- Memory alignment, DMA and zero‑copy considerations for pinned host and device memory.
- Failure/fallback modes to full dequantize/execute when compatibility constraints hit.
- Test matrix and rollout plan for safety canaries.

Background and motivation:
Most of our existing low‑bit exec paths assume batchy, short sequences where dequantization can be done eagerly per request. For streaming long context (hundreds to thousands of tokens) eager full dequantization or synchronously materializing KV for every token adds unacceptable latency and memory churn. In addition, mixed kernel chains (e.g., AWQ attention + INT8 FFN) require coordination to avoid repeated quant/dequant copies. IDB is a producer/consumer pattern that allows kernels to operate on partially dequantized slices while preserving compact on‑device storage and enabling progressive materialization for downstream kernels.

High level design:
1) Logical buffers
   - QuantStore: source-of-truth compressed weight/activation store (immutable for model weights, append-only for streaming activations).
   - IDB (Interleaved Dequant Buffer): an on‑device ring of fixed-size slots. Each slot holds a small dequantized slice (float16/float32 depending on kernel) plus a tiny provenance header. Slots are reused in circular fashion.
   - KVShadow: compact low‑bit KV shard that remains in quantized form until a downstream consumer kernel requires dequantized values.

2) Producer/consumer model
   - Producer kernel (e.g., attention compute that reads QuantStore weights) writes dequantized slices into next free IDB slot. It sets header: sequence_id, token_idx_range, precision_tag, producer_kernel_id, ready_bit.
   - Consumer kernel (e.g., FFN or next attention that needs KV in dequantized dense form) claims the slot via atomic compare-exchange on ready_bit -> busy_bit, consumes data, and records its dependency in per‑slot provenance.
   - When all expected consumers mark consumed, slot is recycled.

3) Partial materialization strategy
   - We do not force dequantization of entire KV rows. Producers pick a window (e.g., last N keys or token chunk) based on token arrival patterns. For long contexts we materialize a sliding window near the tail and keep older KV in quant form in KVShadow.

Quant format constraints and kernel contracts:
- INT8: dequantization to float16 preferred for attention key/query multiplications. Kernel authors must accept float16 input or provide path that consumes INT8 with per‑row scale/bias. IDB supports float16 slots to save memory.
- FP8: may be kept in FP8 format in QuantStore; dequantization uses a 1:1 mapping to float16 when needed. For FP8 kernels that operate directly on FP8 we still publish an ephemeral float16 view for multi‑kernel compatibility.
- GPTQ/AWQ: weight grouping and nonuniform scales are common. Producer must attach a compact reprovision header listing group sizes and scale table id. Consumer kernels that cannot handle grouped dequant must request an expanded slot (runtime will trigger a wider dequantization path).

Kernel ABI additions (minimal):
- idb_acquire(slot_mask) -> slot_handle (string id)
- idb_release(slot_handle)
- idb_header_read(slot_handle) -> sequence_id, token_range, precision_tag, scale_table_id
- idb_flags: {zero_copy, pinned_host, dma_pending}
- schedule_hint: producer may attach schedule_hint with expected consumer latency requirement to influence scheduler placement.

Scheduler implications and placement heuristics:
- Affinity: Producer and hot consumers should be co‑located on same device where possible to avoid costly PCIe/NVLink copies. Scheduler should try to collocate kernels with matching schedule_hint and overlapping token ranges.
- Spill policy: if IDB slots exhausted, scheduler has three options in order: 1) expand slots (allocate more device memory if capacity allows), 2) force synchronous dequant (materialize into temporary buffer passed directly to consumer and bypass IDB), 3) fall back to quantized single‑kernel that does both dequant+consume inline (higher latency but lower memory). The policy is configurable per tenant.

KV cache alignment and multi‑GPU sharding:
- Sharding invariant: KVShadow remains sharded by token range. Each shard maintains its own IDB ring for local producers. Cross‑shard consumers (rare) must use explicit DMA operations and will be scheduled with higher priority to avoid stalling streaming tail.
- Slot indexing: slots include global_kv_shard_id to prevent accidental consumption by out‑of‑shard consumers.
- Consistency: For replication/dual‑redundant setups, producers must publish a lightweight proof (hash) in header to aid cross‑replica reconciliation when head‑tail merging occurs.

Memory layout and DMA considerations:
- Slot size is configurable; recommended default is 16KB per slot (fits typical attention head chunk for 8–64 heads). Choose float16 storage for dequantized slices to reduce memory while keeping numeric stability.
- Use pinned host staging for DMA transfers when device memory is under pressure. IDB supports a 'pinned_host' flag for slots which allows async DMA and double buffering semantics.
- Encourage zero‑copy when consumer kernel supports direct device pointer consumption; support a zero_copy header bit that lets scheduler bypass host copies.

Fallback and compatibility paths:
- Missing scale table: if consumer cannot find scale_table_id referenced, runtime triggers full expand dequant (slower) or falls back to model variant that uses per‑layer uniform quant (configurable).
- Kernel mismatch: if a consumer kernel does not implement IDB ABI, the scheduler detects it at compile/deploy time and inserts an adapter kernel that does a synchronous convert + copy.
- Memory pressure: if all fallback options exhausted and the request cannot be served within latency SLO, runtime will trigger canary fallback to a higher precision hosted model and return degraded but correct output.

Telemetry and observability signals to add:
- idb_slot_alloc_rate, idb_slot_recycle_latency, idb_contention_events (count of CAS failures), idb_dma_duration, idb_pinned_host_rate, idb_consumer_wait_avg.
- Metrics broken down by quant format and tenant to surface format-specific inefficiencies (e.g., GPTQ-heavy workloads causing more expand events).
- Tracing span: idb:produce:id -> idb:consume:id for end‑to‑end latency per slot.

Test matrix (minimal):
- Unit tests: header roundtrip, producer->consumer CAS semantics, slot reuse correctness under heavy concurrency.
- Integration tests: producer/consumer co‑located on GPU; consumer remote on different GPU (DMA path); pinned_host path with forced device OOM to exercise host staging.
- Compatibility tests: INT8 floathalf path, FP8 direct path, GPTQ expand path, AWQ grouped scale path.
- Regression: streaming long context (2k+ tokens) with sliding window materialization and verify steady state memory usage and per‑token latency under load.

Safety/canary rollout plan:
1) Internal alpha: run IDB enabled for internal noncritical tenants with high telemetry sampling.
2) Beta with opt‑in tenants: enable for a subset of production traffic where models are known to be GPTQ/AWQ heavy.
3) Per‑tenant SLA guardrails: ability to disable IDB at runtime if idb_consumer_wait_avg exceeds threshold.
4) Full rollout after 6–8 weeks of stable telemetry.

Open questions / next steps:
- Should float16 be the universal dequant target or support mixed float16/float32 slot types? Tradeoff: simpler kernels vs numeric stability at extreme sequence lengths.
- Fine‑grained eviction policy: can we predict consumer set for a slot to reduce unnecessary expands? Consider integrating with prompt routing / user session hints.
- Security: ensure provenance headers are sanitized and do not leak tenant metadata across shared GPUs.

Action items:
- [ ] Prototype IDB ring and kernel ABI stubs - Miguel (2 weeks)
- [ ] Add scheduler affinity hints and basic spill policy - Eve (3 weeks)
- [ ] Implement telemetry counters and tracing spans - Ayesha (1 week)
- [ ] Create integration tests and run against long‑context harness - Daniel (3 weeks)

Notes to reviewers:
This doc intentionally trades off some implementation detail for conceptual clarity. Kernel authors should treat the IDB ABI as a lightweight contract — the runtime will provide adapters where feasible, but native kernel support gives the best latency. Expect follow‑up PRs with API protos and a small reference kernel pair (producer + consumer) to validate the design.

Appendix: example slot header (human readable)
- sequence_id: UUID string
- token_range: "[start,end)"
- precision_tag: "FP16_FROM_INT8" | "FP16_FROM_FP8" | "FP32"
- scale_table_id: short id or empty
- producer_kernel: "attn_v1"
